blocks.text: At HCL Technologies, people once tried to predict a business review from what the boss was wearing. Forbes India reported the office legend in 2009. A suit and tie meant a good day. An open-neck T-shirt meant get out of the way. Sleeves rolled up and jacket off meant trouble, and fresh cookies in the room were a good sign.
Company legend, not a rule. But people really read his clothes.

The same report says key executives were “petrified” of his “volatile temperament”, and that it called him “the original pit bull terrier” of Indian IT. In 2011 an aide told a Business Standard reporter that the boss was a “softie” at heart. Nadar smiled and did not deny it. He then said he could tolerate mediocrity but not a lack of passion for the work.
I have been severe on myself in my pursuit of perfection and I expect my colleagues to roll up their sleeves and push the boundaries.
The founder who checked the bank every day

In the early years there was no job too small for him. Cash was so tight that he visited one bank every day to see what had been debited and credited. When HCL applied for a loan at Syndicate Bank, he took the first meeting because he was Managing Director. Then a fellow director stayed behind to finish the documents and get the loan. __Do any work yourself, but never do all of it yourself.__

That second half was deliberate. Nadar wrote that most entrepreneurs fail to create enough “bandwidth”, meaning enough capable people to share the load. HCL put an organisation structure in place before it even had office space.
How he hired when he had nothing

In 1976 Nadar was 31 and the oldest person in the company. He told Wharton he did not even have a table of his own. So how do you get a top graduate to join an attic? HCL offered ==₹2,000 a month==, which he said was more than Citibank paid, and every candidate first heard one blunt line: “You should know the size of the company you are joining.”

For example: because the pay was so high, each new hire added 5% to company overhead. So the founders studied every candidate closely. For sales jobs there was barely an interview at all. They drew up role-play charts and told the graduate: “Now, you are the salesman, sell to me.”
He tested salespeople by making them sell. Steal this today.

Engineers were won a different way. Indian Institute of Technology graduates who went to the US often never did real design work, Nadar wrote, while at HCL they could lay hands on a microprocessor and design something. Co-founder Ajai Chowdhry said the founders looked for people with a “cowboy” spirit. __Great people will accept a bad office if the work is rich.__

For example: one night Kiran dragged him to a 10 p.m. film at the Paras cinema in Nehru Place. Afterwards he saw the lights still on at the eighth-floor HCL office and grumbled about the waste. She told him: “I think everybody else is working except you, who has taken his young wife out for a film.” The lift had stopped, so they walked up. Everyone was still there.
How a decision got made

Nadar's rule was that ideas must come up, and then he decides. “I don’t just decide. First it has to be proposed by the CEO and his team. Once I take a decision, everyone else falls in line,” he told Forbes India in 2019. CFO Anil Chanana, who retired in 2018, would say he might not agree with Nadar but would go along with his instincts. On the $1.8 billion IBM software deal, the first payment was due on 30 June, and Chanana sent it a day early just to be safe.

In the boardroom he was unusually careful about his own voice. He told BusinessLine that the moment he says he favours something, he has effectively proposed it, and nobody will argue against the founder's own money. So the CEO or CFO has to propose, and he stays quiet while the others speak. He also stayed out of audit committee meetings and said its chairman “is more powerful than me”.
If you have excellent people then you have to give them the power.

Independent director Amal Ganguli noticed the same habit years earlier. “At times he avoids meetings because when he is present, people at the company defer to him,” Ganguli said in 2009. This was a man whose family then held about 60% of the company.
He skipped meetings because people deferred to him. Founders, think about that.
Picking stars, then backing them

His most famous pick was Vineet Nayar, who joined in 1985 as a trainee. In 1991 Nayar told Nadar over cocktails at a Mumbai hotel that he planned to leave and start something. The two talked all night, flew to Delhi, talked at the office, then talked all night again at Nadar's home. Nayar stayed, and Nadar built a new company, HCL Comnet, for him to run.

For example: when Nayar got bored of selling, Nadar asked him for a business plan. Forbes India says the plan ranged from ready-to-eat omelettes to aircraft manufacturing to satellite communications. Nadar chose satellites. That unit later gave HCL Technologies its remote infrastructure business, which grew from $70 million to $355 million between 2005 and 2009.

Nadar says he told the board in 1999 that Nayar would one day succeed to the top job. When the moment came in 2005 Nayar said no, calling himself the wrong candidate because he had never run a large company. “Shiv is very persuasive,” Nayar later recalled: “a few long dinners and months later, I agreed.” He asked for one thing, a free hand, and Forbes India says he went on to undo much of what his mentor had built.
Stars should not come through a process. They should flicker and they should be visible from a distance.
What working for him was like

The people who worked with him describe two things at once: fear and loyalty. Nayar said Nadar's “mind was way beyond what he was doing” and that he could see potential “that I could not see myself”. NIIT co-founder Rajendra Pawar, a former HCL planner, said: “He can look at the 30,000 feet vision but then be immaculately detailed.” Consultant T.R. Madan Mohan remembered “a certain sharpness in board reviews”.

His view of accountability was simple. An executive can be fired and can be fairly rewarded, he said, but “for doing his job he does not require anyone’s sanctions”. Asked in 2011 about his managers, he said they were doing an excellent job, then added: “If they were not, I would have changed them.” By 2009 HCL Technologies kept a board-approved backup for each of its 26 corporate officers.

It was not all clean. Forbes India's 2009 reporting found that the CFO reported to Nadar rather than to CEO Nayar, and that a nephew running the BPO unit also sat outside Nayar's line. An unnamed senior executive described a formal and an informal organisation running on parallel tracks. A Forrester analyst said HCL's success was “too personality centric”.
Where his hours went

We found no reliable account of a minute-by-minute daily routine, so we will not invent one. What he has said on the record is striking enough. In 2009, at 64, he told Forbes India: “I still work 18 hours a day.” Yet 80% of it went to the university he was building, and he had visited only five of HCL Technologies' 23 country offices, while he went to his school in Uttar Pradesh every month.

blocks.text: 1. Be afraid, but do not obey the fear

Nadar has said Andy Grove's book Only the Paranoid Survive is close to his heart. The test came in 2001 and 2002, when the US economy fell and Nasdaq touched about one-fifth of its peak. About ==76% of HCL's revenue== then came from the US. He says the company was pushed into a corner, so it invested in engineering and R&D services for its healthcare and aerospace customers. By 2014-15 that line brought in 17.1% of revenue.
I am fearful, but I do not act on fear.
blocks.who: Shiv Nadar, writing in Business Today, 2014

blocks.text: Fear is information. It is not a boss.
2. Bet on what does not exist yet

“In those days, we would make business plans on the announced architecture itself,” Nadar told Forbes India. That means HCL planned products around chips that had been announced, before final commercial versions were out. Chowdhry says the first computer was sold before it was fully designed: “We had a brochure and a mock-up of the machine. That was it.” The first orders came from IIT Kharagpur and IIT Madras.

Asked why a young company kept going against the crowd, he gave a four-word answer: “We had no mental baggage.” He also criticised Indian IT firms for bragging each quarter about headcount. He compared it to shooting a football in a room: it hits some wall, and whichever firm owns that wall claims a goal. One tenet he left for young founders reads: “Ensure that your aspirations exceed your resources.”
3. Learn to say no

“When Laxmi comes to your doorstep, it is difficult to close the door,” is the spirit of what he told Wharton in 2006, and he admitted HCL once said yes to far too much. In 30 years, he said, “at least two years had to be written off because of that.” In 2006 he wanted to cut customers from 500 to about 300, which he knew was the reverse of how most companies think. __If saying yes to one customer can cost you ten, no is a growth strategy.__

For example: a client once asked HCL for help with high-precision manufacturing of aircraft-class aluminium. HCL first tried to turn it down because it did not know metallurgy, and the job turned out to be enormously profitable. Nadar's test is about strengths, not comfort: “Unknown business does not scare us because that’s what we’ve done all our lives.”
4. Greed is the enemy of focus

Indian business families often jump into every industry they can. Nadar could have done the same inside IT alone, but he told Forbes India what stops him: “any time I let greed take over, it will destroy this company.” He knows this from experience. He once went into granite and considered aquaculture when it was fashionable in the south. “These were some of our mistakes. But then we were also quick to learn and exit,” he said in 2001.
Granite. A computer company tried granite. Everyone has a granite phase.
5. Build a structure that does not need you

Nadar calls building the organisation his biggest achievement. He learnt a lot of it by watching Hewlett-Packard from a ringside seat after the 1991 partnership, and he invited HP executives into HCL's management and board. HCL had a remuneration committee from 1999, long before the rules pushed everyone towards one, he points out. __A founder's real product is the machine that keeps running after he leaves the room.__
The structure carries them, no single individual should, that's the strength.
6. Stay with partners in their bad years

Toshiba's machines had a 27% share in India through HCL when, by Nadar's numbers, its highest share anywhere else was 2%. He said the partnership had lasted 25 years, including the stretch when Toshiba fell behind in mobile computing. “We may be bad businessmen, but we don’t look at leaving our partners as a possibility,” he said. He also said most people make poor partners because “their mental script has a defect”: they think focus means looking after only themselves.

Be fair about this rule. Not every partnership lasted, and the group parted from Hewlett-Packard and Perot Systems. Its telecom venture with Singapore Telecom failed. The belief is real, but it did not stop hard endings.
7. Think in ten-year plans and bet on hidden talent

“Whatever we aspire to do has to be big to keep my interest in it alive,” he told Wharton in 2010. He runs giving like a company: a 10-year plan, a 10-year budget, a strong board, then metrics checked week by week. He said he studied how the Gates Foundation works like a business. He rejects spending a slice of annual profit on causes because that creates projects, and projects stop.
Talent is randomly distributed. It doesn't look at caste, it doesn't look at creed, it doesn't look at religion, it doesn't look at where you are studying and where you are living.
blocks.who: Shiv Nadar, to Knowledge at Wharton, 2010

blocks.text: For example: VidyaGyan takes top rural students from poor families in Uttar Pradesh and pays for everything. Forbes India reported that ==2.5 lakh children== competed for about 300 places in one year. The student day starts at 5 a.m. and work starts at 5:45. Nadar wants some of them to go into the civil service or run for office.

He rarely talks about himself, but a few stories come from his own words. He was the seventh of eight children, and the family lost his father very young. His father, Sivasubramaniya Nadar, had been a judge, and that is why the family kept moving around Tamil Nadu. His mother raised the children almost alone, and even in hard times she set money aside to give away.

He met Kiran in Delhi in the early 1970s. She was in advertising and he was a client, the Financial Times reports. “Fell in love with my wife, who is a Punjabi and therefore completely different in terms of language,” was how this Tamil engineer told it to Wharton. They married around 1975, according to EducationWorld. Dataquest says she was among those who pushed him to start his own venture.

Kiran built a serious career of her own. She worked at the agency MCM, helped shape the NIIT brand in its early years and, according to EducationWorld, was a promoter-director there from 1982 to 1985. She later played international bridge and won a bronze for India at the 2018 Asian Games. In 2010 she opened the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art, with no formal art training.

For example: she once bought a graphic male nude, “Runners” by Rameshwar Broota. “My husband was horrified!” she told the FT. She felt so crestfallen that she told him they would have to visit the studio and apologise. He met the artist, and then told her she was right to have the painting. “And it is in his study to this day.”
Marry someone who can change your mind about a painting.
The sentence that changed everything

When Hewlett-Packard bought its stake in HCL, the founders came into serious money. Nadar, in his 40s, planned to put his share back into the business. One evening he told his mother and wife his plans. His mother asked: “Why don’t you give some of this back to society, maybe build something more than just HCL?”

“What my mother said struck me like lightning,” he wrote. When he asked what to give, he looked at himself and answered with one line: “I’m a product of education.” He had studied engineering on a scholarship at PSG College, whose founders' trust taught him what lasting giving looks like. The Foundation began in 1994, and in 1996 came the SSN College of Engineering, named after his father.
Never is the time right for charity. Waiting for the right time, it would be to stand in front of sea and wait for the tides to die before taking a dip.
blocks.who: Shiv Nadar, as recorded by the Chennai International Centre, 2023

blocks.text: To put that in scale: in 2024-25 the number two on the list, Mukesh Ambani and family, gave ₹626 crore. The Nadars gave more than four times that. Counting only personal giving, they gave ₹2,537 crore and still ranked first. It was the fourth time in five years they topped the list.

He did not just promise. In June 2010 he sold 2.5% of HCL Technologies and put the whole ₹585 crore into his philanthropic work, Dataquest reported. In 2011 he said 11% of his wealth was set aside. By 2013 he said it looked like 20%, and in 2014 he revealed a personal commitment of a billion dollars. His one regret, stated in 2009: “I wish I had gotten onto philanthropy a lot earlier.”
He was still sorry he started too late. He started in his 40s.

Not everyone applauds the model. When VidyaGyan opened in 2009, Wharton reported that its costs raised eyebrows in a country where rural schools can lack a blackboard, and one critic feared it would become “an island of success”. Nadar himself admits it is built for a chosen few. He calls this “creative” philanthropy, and accepts that it is less scalable but aims to create people who can change the world.

photo.caption: Shiv Nadar (left) laughing with US Ambassador Richard Verma at Shiv Nadar University, 2015.
photo.author: U.S. Embassy New Delhi

blocks.text: His daughter, the only child

Roshni is his only child. When she came to study, he insisted she should live abroad alone for a year and work: “You live abroad for a year alone and work in a company just by yourself.” She took a job at Sky News in London, and no one there knew who she was. She came back in 2008 at 27 wanting to join the Foundation, and that started what he calls his second innings in philanthropy.

Family stays close to the work. Her husband, Shikhar Malhotra, is a director of HCLTech and CEO of HCL Healthcare, and he is Chancellor of Shiv Nadar University. Nadar has shown a soft side about his family only rarely. In 2014 he explained a village development plan by comparing it to his grandson's Lego set. A journalist also saw his stern CEO face change when he spoke about his daughter.

Illness has shaped HCL's history through others. A co-founder's heart surgery led Nadar to decide to shut HCL America. Another co-founder's illness opened the door for Nayar in 2005. Nadar has told one family story about pain: he stormed into an operating theatre shouting at doctors treating his mother's broken bone. A doctor friend told him: “Shiv, if we don’t do this, she will never be able to recover.” He has not made his own health a public subject, and we do not guess.
How he spends and how he relaxes

He is not a monk. Fortune India calls him a private person who made headlines in 2014 for paying ₹115 crore for a bungalow in Delhi. Forbes India noted Armani suits and a love of single malt whisky. Yet a BusinessLine journalist who flew with him on a 12-seat company jet in 2013 found him in a woollen kurta, pyjama and sandals, with no iPad or BlackBerry in sight.

That reporter also learned he is “an ardent movie buff”. In just a few days he had watched an old Tamil film and the Bollywood thriller Race 2. His friends and colleagues have called him “magus”, an old Persian word for a wizard. And at a 2023 talk in Chennai, the moderator mentioned that he had also renovated the Kamakshi temple at Kanchipuram.

chapters.title: The Man Who Hid From Cameras

blocks.text: For most billionaires, the brand is the face. Nadar's brand strategy looked like the opposite. Dataquest called him “the reclusive Shiv Nadar” in 2005. Forbes India's editor wrote in 2009 that he avoided media interactions and was even reluctant to be photographed. In 2011 he began a Business Standard chat by saying he was usually reticent about talking to the media.

For example: in 2019 a Forbes India reporter sat down with him in his 14th-floor office. Nadar pointed at his communications executive and said: “She’s managed to get me in front of you, but I’m media shy.” This was 43 years after he had founded the company.

He was not shy because he was gentle. Forbes India compared the three giants of Indian IT: Narayana Murthy cultivated a statesman's image, Azim Premji came across as a recluse, and Nadar was the fierce one. Mint wrote in 2020 that he rarely hogged the limelight the way the other two did in the public story. So the man who gives most on the Hurun list is often the least known of the three.
You can be famous for giving and still hate cameras.
He let others do the talking

When HCL Technologies paid £441 million for the British firm Axon in 2008, beating Infosys in the middle of the crash, the founder was not at the press conference. Nayar did the talking. Nayar also danced to Bollywood songs at town halls, blogged for Harvard Business Review and sold the slogan “Employees First, Customers Second”. Forbes India said Harvard and Darden began teaching HCL as a case study.

__Nadar's sharpest public-relations move may have been knowing he was not the right voice.__ The old HCL Technologies had a reputation for fierce ways, with high staff attrition and a stock option plan nobody fully understood. A new story needed a new storyteller. Nayar has given the credit back, saying the transformation was Nadar's doing and that of a brilliant team.
But the company knew how to advertise

Reclusive founder, loud marketing. HCL announced its 8C computer through large newspaper ads, at ₹83,500, perhaps the costliest product then advertised in newspapers, according to Dataquest. By its account, the same newspapers carried news that IBM was leaving India. Getting the name itself took salesmanship: the Uttar Pradesh partner wanted “Uttar Pradesh Computers”, and Nadar talked them into Hindustan Computers.

For example: in 1982 HCL's team went into the field with a ₹3 lakh computer, about the price of five top-line Ambassador cars, sold on instalments of ₹3,000 with the tagline “Even your typist can operate it.” Nadar recalled one sale to Dharampal Satyapal, makers of Baba Zarda. The machine was customised so the firm could store the zarda formula on it.
They sold fear of typists to tobacco makers. Marketing genius.
How he talks when he does talk

Rediff described him as soft-spoken, and his reported lines are short and dry. Asked how HCL would handle smaller rivals, he said a big firm is an elephant and a small one a deer. Then came the warning: “Deer have to remember that they can’t and shouldn’t come in the elephant’s way too often.” Asked in 2009 whether his baby was in safe hands, he replied: “Not just two but many.”

He also puts names where they will last. The college carries his father's initials, the school VidyaGyan takes its name from his wife's grandparents, the museum carries Kiran's name and the university his own. He has said which legacy he wants: “I will be known as Shiv Nadar, the philanthropist who also founded HCL, for posterity.” At a 2023 talk, he said the SSN institutions would outlive him and that is what he would be known for.

We found no verified personal social media account in his name. The official accounts belong to HCLTech, the HCL Group and his institutions. For a founder of the internet age that sounds odd, but it fits a career of avoiding the spotlight, and it means any account posing as him deserves suspicion.
India and the world see different men

In India he is first a giving story. He received the Padma Bhushan in 2008, and headlines on his donations now run every year. Tamil Nadu sees him as its own, which is why a Chennai audience asked in 2023 why the university went to Uttar Pradesh. His answer was practical: “Support from bureaucracy in UP was a good reason for me to establish Shiv Nadar University there.” He has even called Uttar Pradesh his “home state”, because HCL became its largest private employer.

Abroad, the company is far better known than the man. Wharton interviewed him twice, Forbes Asia profiled him among its heroes of philanthropy, BNP Paribas gave him its grand prize for individual philanthropy in 2013, and Carnegie Mellon named a professorship for him in 2012. Rediff reported that during his 1996 India visit, Bill Gates held a private meeting with Nadar alone. Nayar believes geography capped the story.
If Shiv was in California, HCL would have been a $500-billion company by now.

blocks.text: Nadar is unusually open about his mistakes, which makes this chapter easier and more useful. We have split it in two. First come his own bad calls. Then come the legal and regulatory fights around his companies, many of them from years when he had stepped back from daily operations.
The $175 million no

In 2000 the Indian IT stars were roughly equal. Infosys, Wipro and HCL Technologies all had revenue of about $200 million. Nadar thought Y2K and routine application work were low value. He even refused a $175 million deal because it paid $28 an hour. By 2005, Infosys had passed $1.5 billion and Wipro was near $1.35 billion, while HCL Tech was about halfway there.

blocks.text: Read his two statements side by side. To Forbes India in 2009 he said: “I never felt bad about losing out to my peers.” To Business Standard in 2011 he called it a “big mistake” and said: “We could have easily become number one had we grabbed that opportunity.” Both can be true. __Y2K was boring work that opened the door to big American clients, and he judged the work without pricing the door.__
Very important for first-time founders! Boring work can buy you the relationship.

He names a bigger miss too: “we missed the bus of being a Microsoft. Our operating system was working in 1977.” HCL had the technology early but was selling hardware in a licence-bound India. He told Wharton the toughest challenge was not building computers but getting government permission to make them. So some of the failure was his, and some was the country's.
A graveyard of products

items.text: Of HCL's five early products, the minicomputer “failed miserably” and the cash register “bombed”.
A client-server product fails: far ahead of what Indian buyers needed.
A small Madras software-export unit flops and is disbanded.
HCL America is ordered shut after a big order is cancelled. Customers refuse to lose the engineers, and he reverses the decision.
Granite, an aquaculture plan and a telecom venture with Singapore Telecom are written off as mistakes or failures.
HCL Infosystems decides to wind up the PC business that started it all.

blocks.text: Notice what saved them. The 8-bit system ran for 12 years, a data-entry product for 15, and a programmable calculator “kept the fireplace going”, Nadar wrote. HCL won because some bets paid for the rest. Note the HCL America story too: the closure team went to shut it down, and customers offered to pay the engineers' salaries. That near-death experience pointed the way to software services.
Holding the steering wheel too long

In 2006 Wharton asked what he would do differently. Forbes India would later describe a company he ran so tightly that people feared the reviews, with staff attrition among the highest in the industry. His answer is the most useful sentence in this book for a young founder.
I could have taken my hands off the steering wheel a lot earlier and delegated more authority than I did.
blocks.who: Shiv Nadar, to Knowledge at Wharton, 2006

blocks.text: To his credit, he did step aside, and the numbers show what that did. Under Nayar, Outlook Business reported, HCL Tech went from $700 million in revenue to about $4.5 billion in six years, and market value rose from a low of $1.4 billion to over $10 billion. Letting go was the best business decision in his career. The hard part is that it came after five years of falling behind.
The first child that faded

HCL Infosystems was the hardware company he built first. “I knew every brick of that building,” he said. By 2013 its leaders said a rejig was needed “to save the company”. Analysts said about 80% of revenue depended on selling Nokia handsets, and Nokia had already taken half of the distribution back in the mid-2000s. Its shares had fallen more than 80% in five years by January 2013.

It lost ₹214.52 crore in the year to June 2014. Its auditors' report for March 2026 says it has made losses for several years, that its net worth is fully eroded, and that there is material uncertainty about its ability to continue as a going concern. Fair context matters here: the PC business faced thin margins, imported parts and a global shift to phones. __Never let one customer become your whole company.__
Read this twice. One customer is not a business. It is a job.
The ₹820 crore tax fight

In June 1999, months before the HCL Technologies IPO, three Nadar holding companies sold 70 lakh shares to a Mauritius company, Wintech, at ₹50 each. Income-tax officers raided HCL offices in January 2002. They argued the price was far too low and valued the shares at ₹1,807, adding about ₹1,229.9 crore to income, with tax demands of over ₹800 crore. A tribunal first ordered interim payments of ₹100 crore plus ₹15 crore a month.

HCL said the sale was properly valued and disclosed. In March 2006 the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal in Delhi ruled that these additions were not sustainable and were beyond the scope of that type of assessment. It partly allowed HCL's appeal. It did not decide what the shares were truly worth, calling that question academic. A chartered accountant filed a public-interest petition in 2009 raising the same route, and we could not find its outcome.
Winning on legal grounds is not the same as proving the price.
HCL in other people's scandals

In 2011 UK MPs investigating the News International phone-hacking scandal questioned HCL, which handled some of the group's data-centre work. HCL first said it had never stored the data and so could not have deleted it. It then told MPs it knew of hundreds of thousands of emails deleted at the client's request, in nine episodes between April 2010 and July 2011. Its lawyers said it saw nothing “abnormal, untoward or inconsistent with its contractual role”.

In 2019 Bloomberg reported that Boeing and its subcontractors had used lower-paid temporary engineers, including from HCL, on 737 MAX work, some earning as little as $9 an hour. Boeing said it did not rely on HCL or Cyient engineers for the MCAS system blamed in the two crashes or for the cockpit warning-light fix. HCL declined to comment on its specific work. We found no finding against HCL in the sources we read.
Clients and courts

In March 2017 brewer MillerCoors sued HCL in Illinois, seeking more than $100 million over a software project worth about $53 million that it said ran late and was understaffed. HCL said it was seeking an amicable settlement. After settlement talks in court, the case was dismissed with prejudice by joint request in November 2018. The docket we read does not show any terms.

American workers and applicants brought other cases. A 2019 suit alleging HCL favoured South Asian workers and misused visas settled in principle in 2021, with terms not public. A separate whistleblower case claimed underpayment of H-1B workers: HCL denied it, and in January 2025 a US appeals court upheld dismissal. That ruling rested on the False Claims Act, and it did not decide whether visa rules were broken.

For example: in April 2026 HCL America agreed to pay ==$495,000== to settle a US government lawsuit. The EEOC said a qualified 62-year-old applicant of Indian descent was rejected in 2021, with an email to the hiring team saying he was “too old”. Under the two-year decree, HCL America must also revise its policies and train its recruiters. A separate 2020 California suit alleged caste-linked bias; we could not find an outcome.
“Employees First”, and the fine print

The slogan has been tested at home too. In 2009, with the recession biting, Business Standard reported a pay freeze, cut bonuses, and reported job reductions, with a source saying staff were being charged for coffee. Nayar has since recalled that the firm would not fire anyone during the slowdown. In January 2022 union NITES complained HCL was clawing back pre-paid bonuses from people who resigned, up to ₹1.7 lakh, and sometimes holding back documents.

HCL said the matter was incorrectly reported, then revoked the repayment rule from 22 December 2021 while pursuing earlier sums, and told the Labour Commissioner its contract gave it the right. We could not find a final ruling. In 2023 NITES complained again about a bonus being tied back to performance, and HCL said it was simply returning to its pre-pandemic policy.
What a young founder should not copy

blocks.title: Do not rule by fear
blocks.text: People checking your shirt before a meeting is not a good sign. It is a warning that the truth is not reaching you.

blocks.title: Do not price only the first deal
blocks.text: He judged Y2K work by its hourly rate. His rivals judged it by the clients it opened.

blocks.title: Do not keep power in private channels
blocks.text: A formal and informal organisation running side by side confuses everyone, however good your new CEO is.

blocks.title: Do not say Employees First and then surprise employees
blocks.text: A slogan raises the standard you will be judged by. Every pay or bonus change gets read against it.

On 11 August 2026 the HCL Group turned 50. Its founder is 81, and he is no longer the person running it. HCLTech's annual report lists him as Founder and Chairman Emeritus and Strategic Advisor to the Board. He has no board seat, and the Shiv Nadar University lists him as Founder and former Chancellor. HCL Corporation's website still lists him as a director.

items.text: Vineet Nayar becomes president of HCL Technologies, then CEO in 2007.
Nadar steps down as chairman; Roshni takes over.
At 76 he resigns as MD and director, and begins a five-year term as Chairman Emeritus.
Gift deeds move 47% of each holding company to Roshni. His own share falls to 4%, and hers rises to 57.33%.
HCL marks 50 years. The AGM highlights ₹1,30,144 crore revenue and a ₹60 dividend per share.

blocks.text: The handover is worth studying because it reversed his own words. In 2011 he said of the IT business: “I know the industry inside out; my daughter doesn’t. So she can’t play the role that I have played.” In 2014 he said she would be part of governance but not operations. That line has held: Roshni chairs as a non-executive while C. Vijayakumar runs the company as CEO and Managing Director.
He separated owning from running. Most family firms never manage this.

blocks.text: The bets being made now

HCLTech says it wants to be the world's best AI solutions provider. It reported ==$620 million== of annualised “Advanced AI” revenue for 2025-26, $688 million by the first quarter of the next year, and more than $700 million by October 2026. It has taken over 10% of Indian AI firm Sarvam and is moving into AI data centres. The plain goal, Business Today says, is to break the old rule that more revenue needs more people.

The most poetic bet is hardware. HCL Group and Foxconn are building India Chip, a 60:40 joint venture in Jewar, Uttar Pradesh, on which the Prime Minister laid the foundation stone in February 2026. It plans to process 20,000 wafers a month into display-driver chips, with about ₹3,700 crore invested and production expected in 2028. Roshni says government incentives will fund around 65-70% of the project. A company that once fought for a licence to make computers is back in manufacturing.

blocks.text: Wealth numbers around him now carry a footnote. He gave away control, yet Forbes still lists him at around $27-31 billion, and Fortune India places the same wealth under Roshni's name, at ₹2,22,976 crore. So treat every ranking of “his” money with care. The dividend number matters more to his story: he explained in 2010 that HCL dividends flow into a family company, and from there a large share goes to the Foundation.
What he says he wants

His recent public record is thin. We found no fresh on-the-record interview from 2025 or 2026. When FICCI gave him a lifetime award for education in October 2025, Roshni collected it for him. Dataquest's report that month counted more than $1.5 billion invested by the Foundation and 39,000 students and alumni served.

So his goals must be read from what he has said over time. In 2014 he predicted that healthcare could become bigger than HCL Tech and education about the same size, both built on new technology. In 2019 he worried: “I don’t think our companies today are capable of taking courageous decisions like we did at that time.” In 2023 he told a Chennai audience that the SSN institutions would outlast him, and that was how he hoped to be known.

The institutions are moving without him at the centre. The village project he called the biggest anyone had dared became HCL Samuday, covering about 90,000 households in Hardoi district, with about ₹100 crore a year from HCL Foundation by 2017. The new Kiran Nadar Museum of Art, designed by Adjaye Associates, is planned for a site near Delhi airport in 2026 or 2027. That is what he said he wanted: things that keep going.
A founder can carry an institution only so far and then others have to step in, even the alumni.

The last word on HCL at 50 went to his daughter, and it sounds like him. “What was relevant in 1976 or even what was relevant a couple of years ago is no longer relevant,” she told Business Today in October 2026. __He spent 50 years building a company that could outgrow every idea he ever had, including the idea that he should run it.__
That is the real exit. Not selling. Being unnecessary.

lessons.title: Check your own cash.
lessons.text: In HCL's early days Nadar went to the bank every day to see the balance, because cash was that tight. Know your number before anyone asks. No dashboard replaces that habit when money is short.

lessons.title: Test people on the job itself.
lessons.text: HCL hardly interviewed its first sales hires. It told them: “Now, you are the salesman, sell to me.” Ask a designer to design and a coder to code before you trust a CV.

lessons.title: Pay for talent before you can afford a table.
lessons.text: In 1976 Nadar had no table of his own, yet he paid ₹2,000 a month, more than Citibank by his account. Each hire added 5% to overhead, so every choice mattered. Spend on the people first and the office last.

lessons.title: Give good people hard, real work.
lessons.text: Top engineers came to HCL because they could actually design with a microprocessor. One night Nadar found the whole office working late, unasked. Rich work keeps people when money cannot.

lessons.title: Say no to work that does not use your strengths.
lessons.text: Nadar says that in 30 years HCL wrote off at least two years because it said yes too often. For one wrong customer you could lose ten. Be polite, and walk away.

lessons.title: Count the full cost of your principles.
lessons.text: He refused a $175 million deal in 2000 because $28 an hour felt too low, and rivals used such work to win big American clients. He later called missing Y2K a big mistake. Boring work is sometimes the entrance fee.

lessons.title: Plan around what is about to exist.
lessons.text: HCL made business plans on chips that had only been announced, and sold its first computer with a brochure and a mock-up. Do not wait for proof that everybody else can also see. Move while it still looks early.

lessons.title: Be afraid, but do not be run by fear.
lessons.text: When 76% of HCL's revenue depended on a collapsing US market in 2001, Nadar built a new engineering business instead of freezing. “I am fearful, but I do not act on fear.” Use panic as a signal to build.

lessons.title: Bury failures quickly.
lessons.text: HCL's minicomputer failed, its cash register bombed, and Nadar quit granite and dropped aquaculture. “We were also quick to learn and exit,” he said. The calculator kept paying the bills while they tried again.

lessons.title: Build the team before you have the office.
lessons.text: Nadar set up an organisation structure before HCL even had office space, then split work among his co-founders. There is only so much one person can do. Divide the load on day one.

lessons.title: Let go earlier than feels safe.
lessons.text: He told Wharton he could have taken his hands off the wheel far sooner. HCL Tech fell behind by 2005, and it only took off once Vineet Nayar got a free hand. Hand over before the numbers force you to.

lessons.title: Keep your opinion back until your team has spoken.
lessons.text: Nadar learned that once the founder says yes, the debate is over. So at board meetings he let the CEO or CFO propose first, and sometimes he skipped meetings altogether. Your silence can be a management tool.

lessons.title: Spot the star, then get out of the way.
lessons.text: When his top salesman got bored in 1991, Nadar talked with him for two nights and then gave him a company. “Stars should not come through a process,” he said. Retain restless people by giving them something bigger.

lessons.title: Never depend on one customer.
lessons.text: HCL Infosystems at one point drew about 80% of revenue from selling Nokia phones, and Nokia took half the distribution back. Its shares fell over 80% in five years. If one client can end you, you do not own a business yet.

lessons.title: Start giving before you feel rich enough.
lessons.text: In his 40s, when his mother asked why he would not give something back, he planned instead to reinvest. She changed his mind, and he later said he wished he had started earlier. Start with what you have today.

factCheck.method: Written from pages read directly on 2 November 2026 through the Exa fetch tool and read-only curl: Nadar's own essays and on-the-record interviews (Wharton, Forbes India, Business Today, BusinessLine, Business Standard, Mint), former colleagues on the record (Vineet Nayar, Rajendra Pawar, Ajai Chowdhry, Amal Ganguli), court and agency records (ITAT Delhi order, US Second Circuit opinion, EEOC release, MillerCoors docket), stock-exchange filings and HCLTech's 2025-26 annual report. Quotes were copied from the page text. Anonymous sources in Forbes India are labelled as unnamed. Allegations in lawsuits are described as allegations, with the outcome when we could find one. Grandchildren are not named, and no home address is given. The Financial Times and Bloomberg Law pieces were read as excerpts only because they are partly paywalled; the Bloomberg 737 MAX report was read through Business Today's summary.

disputed.claim: Was Nadar ever CEO of HCL Technologies?
disputed.note: He told Wharton in 2006 “As the CEO of HCL Technologies, I was a hands-on CEO.” He told Forbes India in 2009 “I never was the CEO” and named S. Raman as co-founder and CEO. strategy+business and Business Standard also call him CEO. His first description and his later one conflict, so we avoid a formal claim and describe how he ran the firm.

disputed.claim: How many IIM Calcutta graduates HCL hired in its early years
disputed.note: Nadar told Wharton in 2006 they hired five students. Forbes India in 2019 says the whole batch turned up one late-1970s year and HCL hired about a hundred. These may be different years. We use neither figure.

disputed.claim: When and how the Hewlett-Packard partnership ended
disputed.note: Rediff says HP bought 26% in 1991 and the two had parted by 2001. Dataquest says the JV broke off in 1996. Forbes India 2019 says a venture called HCL-HP ended after six years in 2014, which looks like an error. Economic Times links the 1994 Foundation to a windfall from HP exiting. Nadar says the stake sale came in his late 40s. We say only that they parted.

disputed.claim: Whether HCL protected jobs during the 2008-09 recession
disputed.note: Nayar told Mint the firm would not fire anyone during the slowdown. Business Standard in April 2009 reported a plan to cut about 280 jobs and about 450 lay-offs in one practice, partly from unnamed sources. It also describes 280 as 8% of the global workforce, which cannot be right for a company of that size. We give both versions and leave out the percentage.

Dataquest gives ₹811 crore and Rediff/Business Standard gives ₹820.44 crore. The tribunal order records additions of ₹1,229.90 crore to income, while Dataquest says ₹1,319 crore. We use the order for the addition and “over ₹800 crore” for the demand. We did not find a later ruling on the Revenue's other remedies or an outcome for the 2009 petition in the Allahabad High Court.

disputed.claim: Who holds the wealth after the March 2025 gift
disputed.note: Filings show he kept 4% of each holding company and Roshni 57.33%. Forbes still lists Nadar at $31.4 billion in real time and $27.4 billion on its India list, while Fortune India lists Roshni at ₹2,22,976 crore. These are publishers' choices about family fortune, not contradictions in the filings. We flag this in the text.

disputed.claim: Whether his Chairman Emeritus term was formally renewed
disputed.note: The 2021 filing gave a five-year term from 20 July 2021. HCLTech's annual report published in July 2026 still lists him in that role, and the August 2026 AGM had no resolution about it. We did not find a filing on a renewal, so we report the title as HCLTech uses it.

Dataquest in October 2025 says more than $1.5 billion. The profile fragment reports over $1.85 billion from the Foundation's homepage, but that site was under maintenance when we checked, so we could not re-read it. Forbes and Fortune India give $1.1 billion. These look like different dates.

Nadar himself told Wharton “My father was a judge”, BusinessLine calls him a former District Judge, and Nadar wrote in Mint that the family lost him very young. This settles the open question in the profile fragment's note on his father's work.

disputed.claim: Age at which he first saw a city
disputed.note: Nadar told Wharton 22. BusinessLine and Outlook say 21 and name Chennai. This is outside our chapters' main story, so we do not state it.

disputed.claim: When and how Nadar and Kiran met
disputed.note: The FT says she was in advertising and he was a client. EducationWorld says they met and married in 1975. Dataquest says he was dating her in the early 1970s. We use “early 1970s” for meeting and “around 1975” for the wedding, with attribution.

disputed.claim: World-first claims for HCL computers and software
disputed.note: Nadar and some Indian outlets describe HCL's 8C as among the first or the first personal computer, and Genesis as ahead of Oracle. Business Standard itself adds that IBM and Apple would disagree. We repeat no world-first claim.

disputed.claim: The private meeting with Bill Gates in 1996
disputed.note: Rediff alone says Nadar was the only person Gates met privately on that visit. We attribute it to Rediff and could not confirm it elsewhere.

disputed.claim: Business-review dress code and the “pit bull” label
disputed.note: Forbes India presents the clothes story as office legend and the “pit bull” label as how observers described him, not as established fact. We label them the same way. Nadar has not confirmed the dress-code story.

disputed.claim: Scale and funding of the village project
disputed.note: Forbes India in 2015 called it Samudhay, with 120 villages and UP government funding planned. Business Standard in 2017 and HCL Samuday's own site describe HCL Samuday in Hardoi, funded by HCL Foundation, at about 720 villages, 164 gram panchayats and 90,000 households. The numbers on the project's reach come from the organisers, not an outside audit.
